notes.meaning: David returned to Ziklag after winning a battle against the Amalekites, staying there for two days. This passage connects directly with the end of First Samuel, showing that David was far away when Saul died. David waited patiently for God to guide his next steps rather than rushing forward to seize the throne.

On the third day, a man arrived from Saul's army with torn clothing and dirt on his head as signs of deep grief. He threw himself on the ground before David to show honor. By doing this, he treated David as the newly recognized leader of Israel.
David asked the traveler where he had come from. The man answered that he had fled from the camp of Israel. His words showed right away that the army was in great trouble.

David asked the runner to explain how the battle turned out. The messenger reported that Israel's troops had fled, many soldiers had died, and both Saul and Jonathan were dead. He singled out Jonathan because Jonathan was the crown prince and next in line for the throne.
David asked the young man how he was sure that Saul and Jonathan had died. He wanted to know whether the messenger had seen their deaths himself or was merely repeating a rumor from the battlefield.

The young man said he happened to be on Mount Gilboa and saw Saul leaning on his spear while enemy chariots closed in around him. Most commentators recognize this story as a lie, since First Samuel clearly states Saul had already fallen on his sword. The messenger had likely wandered onto the battlefield looking for valuables to steal from the dead.
The messenger claimed that Saul turned around, spotted him, and called out to him. The young man answered right away, pretending he had been standing by to assist the wounded king.

When Saul asked him who he was, the young man told him he was an Amalekite. It is striking that an Amalekite stood before Saul, since God had commanded Saul years earlier to wipe out that enemy nation.

The runner claimed Saul begged him to kill him because he was in terrible pain and his life was dragging on. This part of the story was almost certainly made up, because Saul had taken his own life specifically to avoid dying at the hands of foreigners.

The Amalekite claimed he killed Saul and took the king's crown and armband to give them to David. He had reached the body before the Philistines arrived and brought these royal symbols to David, hoping for a rich reward.
When David heard the news, he grabbed his clothes and tore them in deep grief, and his men did the same. Tearing one's clothing was an ancient way to express sudden and overwhelming sorrow.

David and his men wept, mourned, and fasted until evening for Saul, Jonathan, and the fallen soldiers of Israel. Even though Saul had hunted David for years, David truly grieved over the king and the defeat of God's people.
David formally questioned the messenger again about his background. The young man replied that he was the son of an Amalekite immigrant living in Israel.

David asked the man how he could dare to raise his hand to strike down the Lord's anointed king. David viewed the king's life as sacred because God had placed Saul in office, and David himself had twice refused to harm Saul.

differ.view: Some teach that verses about the Lord's anointed mean church leaders should not be questioned or criticized by others.
Many teach that this phrase referred strictly to God's chosen king and protects against physical harm, not against fair and biblical accountability for pastors.

notes.meaning: David ordered one of his young soldiers to execute the messenger, and the soldier struck him down. David acted with lawful authority to punish someone who openly confessed to killing the king.

David told the dying man that his death was on his own head because his own mouth had confessed to killing the Lord's anointed. Whether the runner had lied or told the truth, he was condemned by his own words.
David wrote a funeral poem, called a lament, to honor Saul and Jonathan. It was an expression of real grief that celebrated the fallen heroes and set aside all past grievances.

David directed that the people of Judah be taught this poem, which was titled the Song of the Bow. It was recorded in the Book of Jashar, an ancient collection of Hebrew songs celebrating great leaders and battles.
The song opens with grief over Israel's pride and glory lying dead on the hills of Gilboa. David repeats the cry, 'How the mighty have fallen,' which serves as the main chorus throughout the poem.
David wished the news would never reach the Philistine cities of Gath and Ashkelon. He could not bear the thought of enemy women singing and dancing in victory while mocking the God of Israel.

David called out in poetic sorrow for the mountains of Gilboa to receive no rain or dew, leaving them barren where the tragedy happened. He grieved that Saul's shield was thrown down in disgrace and no longer rubbed with oil as a holy weapon.

David praised the battlefield bravery of Jonathan and Saul, whose bow and sword always struck their targets effectively. Even in their final defeat, David remembered their long record of courage in battle.

David spoke of Saul and Jonathan as united in life and together in death. Though their relationship had faced severe trials, Jonathan remained loyal to his father and died fighting beside him like a lion.

David urged the women of Israel to weep for Saul, who had brought wealth and fine red clothing to the people through his victories. He chose to praise Saul for the prosperity he won for the nation rather than dwell on his personal failings.
David repeated the mournful cry over the fallen soldiers who died in the middle of the fighting. His attention turned directly to Jonathan, who had been slain on Israel's own hills.

David poured out his deep personal pain over Jonathan, whom he called his brother and dearest companion. He described Jonathan's selfless covenant loyalty as extraordinary, surpassing the devotion David had experienced in any other relationship.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern readers attempt to view this verse as describing a romantic or homosexual bond, but biblical scholars reject this, explaining that it describes extraordinary covenant friendship and sacrificial loyalty between warriors.

notes.meaning: David brought the song to an end with one last cry over the fallen heroes and Israel's lost strength. He used the weapons of war as a picture of the noble fighters who had perished.
